HK1: A bad knee is not a knee problem. It is a weight problem, and the weight has to go somewhere.
I fit stair rails for a living. I have been in about four hundred houses and I have watched where it goes.
I need you to take this seriously.
HK2: I can tell how long someone has had a bad knee by which rail they ask me to fit.
The first one goes at the top of the stairs. The second one goes the whole way down.
I would like to stop being called back for the second one.
HK3: When I am asked to move a bed into a front room, the knee has usually been bad for about six years.
Nobody plans for that. It arrives one small change at a time, and I can name every one of them.
BODY: Here is the sequence, and it is almost always the same.
One knee starts hurting on the stairs. So you favour it. You lead with the good leg, every step.
The good leg is now doing the work of two. Within a year or two it starts as well.
Then a rail at the top. Then a rail all the way down. Then you stop going up in the afternoon. Then a bed comes downstairs.
I am not telling you that to frighten you. Every step on that list is a response to weight landing in one place.
Two centimetres below your kneecap there is a band of tendon about as wide as your thumb. Every step you take lands on it. Seventeen times your bodyweight.
Put your finger there and press. That is the band.
Coming down is worse than going up. Going up, your muscles lift you. Coming down, nothing does. You are catching yourself, and the catch lands on that band.
The pain is not the first thing that happened. It is the first thing you noticed.
You have been told it is your age. Or your weight. Or that the muscle is weak. Sometimes that is part of it. It has never been the whole of it.
The physio helps and then stops helping. The gel sits on your skin. The pills switch the alarm off. The sleeve squeezes the whole knee and leaves that band carrying everything.
None of them are wrong. None of them move the weight off the band, and that is the only thing that stops the sequence.
The strap I keep in the van now is called Stryde.

It sits two centimetres below the kneecap, on the tendon. It never crosses the joint. There is a silicone pad inside that holds pressure on that one band instead of spreading it round the whole knee. Your weight gets caught and moved off the worn part before it reaches the joint.
The placement is the whole thing. A little too high and it is a sleeve again.
Thirty four percent less strain. Measured. Three years with orthopedic surgeons. Two hundred thousand people wearing one.
I am not paid by them. I started carrying a couple because I was tired of fitting the second rail.
Three houses this year have not called me back. That is not a study. It is just what I have seen.
Not because the arthritis is gone. It is still there. Because the weight is not landing on that band any more.
You do not have to believe me. One knee only. Leave the other bare. Go to your own stairs and come down forwards. You will know in a minute.
Two for one, so you do both knees, which is the point. Sixty days, and you keep the straps. From the Stryde site. The copies stretch, and a stretched strap does not hold the spot.
And if you know somebody whose stairs have started taking them longer, send them this. That is the one I would rather you did.
